title: Reading slowly
hookLine: reading as practice: one line, then silence
tomorrow: Ananda says friends are half the path. why does the Buddha say no?

lines: BAHIYA STOPS THE BUDDHA IN THE STREET.
cards: A podcast at double speed. A long thread skimmed between classes. Here's a man who couldn't afford to skim.

Bahiya has come a long way to find the Buddha, and he finds him on a street in Savatthi, on the morning alms round, bowl in hand. Bahiya asks to be taught, right there. The Buddha says it isn't the time.
Bahiya asks again: life is uncertain, he says, and so is his. A third time. What can anyone teach on a sidewalk, in the time it takes to say a sentence?

teach.h: A FEW LINES IN THE STREET.
teach.b: The Buddha answers with a few short lines. In the Udana, a collection of short inspired sayings, they run roughly like this: in the seen, let there be only the seen; in the heard, only the heard.
No extra story laid on top. And the text says Bahiya's mind was freed, right there in the street. A few lines, heard all the way down.

The Dhammapada says it as a verse. A thousand empty words are worth less than one word of sense, and in Max Müller's old translation, "one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet." Notice the test.
Not a word he can repeat, or explain, or post.

teach.h: ONE WORD THAT MAKES YOU QUIET.
teach.b: A word that makes him quiet. That's the teaching under the way Buddhists handle their texts.
In temples you'll hear the same short texts chanted again and again, slowly, aloud. The Pali word for it is sajjhaya: recitation. A line isn't finished when you reach the period.
It's finished when it goes quiet in you. Which changes what a reading list is for. Ten texts read fast are ten texts passed.
One line, read slowly and then left alone in silence, can do its whole work.

how: Buddhists read and chant short texts aloud, at home and in temples, often the same verses again and again; some read a single verse before sitting and let it rest in the silence.

o: taking in one line at a time and letting it sink in
studying a text only when a teacher is present

games.q: who did what — tap the pairs.
p: asked three times in the street
answered with a few short lines
better than a thousand empty ones

s: the longer the teaching, the more it can do
the Dhammapada says one word of sense that makes you quiet is better than a thousand empty ones.
in the Udana, Bahiya asks more than once before the Buddha teaches him
the Buddha says it isn't the time; Bahiya asks again, and on the third ask he's taught.
Buddhist texts are meant to be read silently and fast, like a textbook
in temples the same short texts are chanted aloud, slowly, again and again.

games.q: your class has one evening to 'cover' a long Buddhist text. a friend says skim it all tonight. what fits today's teaching?
o: read one short passage aloud, slowly, and sit with it before moving on
split it up so everyone skims a part and posts a summary
skip the text and watch a summary video together instead
games.why: the Dhammapada's test is a word that makes you quiet, not a page count. Bahiya was freed by a few lines, heard fully.

practice: Here's one line for the sit, from that verse: one word of sense is better, which if a man hears, he becomes quiet. Say it once, out loud and slowly. Then stop adding to it, and let the line go quiet for two minutes.

wordCard.voice: Reading slowly: a line read until it goes quiet in you, the way Bahiya heard a few words in the street.

carryVoice: Your line: one line, then silence. Bahiya needed only a sidewalk's worth. See you tomorrow.
